item.text: {"answers":[{"question_id":"Q025_classification_as_evolutionary_hypothesis","answer":"Assign it as a new superfamily within the existing SCOPe fold. In SCOPe terms, sharing a fold says the domain has the same major secondary-structure elements in the same arrangement and with the same topological connections, but it does not by itself claim demonstrable homology. A new superfamily inside that fold is therefore the right level for a domain whose core topology fits a known fold while available sequence, structural-detail, and functional evidence do not convincingly place it in any existing homologous superfamily.\n\nA new family would be too strong if the target merely resembles the fold: a family assignment asserts a close evolutionary relationship to a known family, typically supported by high sequence similarity or very strong lower-sequence evidence, and would make function transfer comparatively safer only within that close homologous context. A new superfamily in an existing fold asserts that the domain belongs to the same fold but starts a separate probable-homology group; it should not be used to transfer detailed active-site chemistry, ligand specificity, or family-level function from neighboring superfamilies just because the fold is shared. A new fold would be too broad a split unless the domain has a genuinely different core architecture/topology that cannot be represented by any existing fold. The SCOPe class level is even coarser, describing broad secondary-structure composition such as all-alpha, all-beta, alpha/beta, or alpha+beta rather than a specific evolutionary hypothesis, so no new class is implicated here.","evidence_used":["pretrained model knowledge"]}]}
